FINAL PATHOLOGIC DIAGNOSIS
A. "Abdominal tumor margin", excision: Fibroadipose tissue with focal
neuroglial tissue, consistent with gliomatosis peritonei.

B. Right ovary, oophorectomy:
1. Serosal involvement by neuroglial tissue, consistent with gliomatosis
peritonei; see comment.
2. Serosal adhesions.

C. Abdominal tumor, excision: Gliomatosis peritonei with increased
cellularity; see comment.
COMMENT:
H&E sections of the abdominal tumor (Parts A and C) show a variably
cellular proliferation of spindle cells with eosinophilic
cytoplasm and open chromatin in a collagenous to myxoid
stroma. Prominent lymphoid aggregates surround the mass. The
differential diagnosis includes fibromatosis, leiomyoma, and glial
tissue (gliomatosis peritonei). Immunohistochemical stains were
performed and evaluated on block C4 with the following results in the
spindle cells:
- GFAP: Positive.
- SOX2: Positive.
This immunostaining pattern confirms that these cells are glial in
origin.
The findings are consistent with gliomatosis but the proliferation is
more cellular than typical cases of gliomatosis. Additional
immunohistochemical stains were performed on block C5 with
the following results:
- ATRX: Retained staining.
- Olig2: Scattered positive.
- MIB-1: Increased staining in a rim of tissue.
- p53: No increase in staining.
- SOX10: Rare positive cells.
The staining results are not specific but are diagnostic of a glioma or
another specific entity.
There are no rosettes or evidence of immature teratoma and the features
are not diagnostic of a glioma. Ultimately, the findings are consistent
with gliomatosis with increased cellularity and proliferative activity.
The significance of these findings is uncertain and close clinical
follow-up should be considered.
Select slides from the patient's prior specimen (S22-3456-C1) are
concurrently reviewed in comparison and show similar features.
Drs. J. Doe, H. Smith (UCSF Pediatric Pathology) and C. Jones (UCSF Neuropathology) have reviewed selected slides and agree with
the diagnosis.

Clinical History
The patient is a 13-year-old boy with history of immature abdominal
teratoma status post resection (S22-3456) who presents with difficulty
in defecation. Imaging showed a hyperintense mass (6.5 x 5.5 x 4.5 cm)
centered in the rectouterine pouch. He undergoes exploratory
laparotomy. Intraoperatively there was a bulky tumor in the abdomen in
the pouch of Douglas and a plaque-like tumor near the left broad
ligament, both of which were resected. The right ovary was scarred to the peritoneum and was also resected.

The case is received in three parts, each labeled with the patient's
name and medical record number.
Part A is received fresh, additionally labeled "abdominal tumor margin
frozen," ("abdominal tumor margin in pouch of Douglas-rectal/sigmoid

tissue (1 x 0.5 x 0.1 cm). The specimen is submitted entirely for frozen
section diagnosis A FS1; the frozen section remnant is submitted in

Part B is received fresh, additionally labeled "R ovary," and
consists of a fragmented ovary (3.5 cm in aggregate length x up to 1 cm in diameter x 0.3 cm in wall thickness). The serosa is pink and
smooth with no discrete cysts or nodules. The fimbriated segment is
hemorrhagic; otherwise, the ovary is unremarkable. The bisected fimbria
are submitted in cassette B1 and the remainder of the tube is cross
sectioned and submitted in cassettes B2 and B3. (nxc)
Part C is received fresh, additionally labeled "abdominal tumor," and
consists of a rubbery pink-tan nodular mass (7 x 5 x 4 cm)
and a free-floating piece of irregular firm pink-tan tissue (3 x 2 x
1 cm). There are multiple white sutures stitched into the mass and

inked black. The cut surfaces of the mass and free-floating piece of
tissue are homogenous, tan-white to yellow and thinly encapsulated.
There are multifocal areas of punctate hemorrhage but no necrosis.
Representative sections of the mass are submitted in cassettes C1-C8 and
representative sections of the free-floating piece of tissue are
submitted in cassettes C9 and C10. (nxc)
